Instructions for submitting Observer reports 

Introduction 
This document provides the reporting template and instructions for Observers to report 

during the 2023 - 2025 Norwegian Chairship of the Arctic Council. 

The deadline for submission is 1 December 2024. 

 

Role of Observers 
The role and responsibilities of Observers, as well as criteria for admission to the Arctic 

Council, can be found in the “Arctic Council Rules of Procedure” (Annex 2) and the 

“Observer Manual for Subsidiary Bodies.” 

The primary role of Observers is to observe the work of the Arctic Council. Observers 
contribute to the Arctic Council primarily through engagement at the level of Working 
Groups, Task Forces, and/or Expert Groups. Observers are invited to the meetings and 
other activities of the Arctic Council unless the Senior Arctic Officials decide otherwise. 
Observers may also propose projects through an Arctic State or a Permanent Participant. 

Report submission 
Observer reports should include the relevant information described below and in the 
template. 

(a) A description of the Observer’s contributions to the work of the Arctic Council since 
the time of the Observer’s most recent submission, or in the previous two years, with 
special focus on contributions to the subsidiary bodies through project participation 
and support, as well as collaboration with Permanent Participants; 

(b) If applicable, a description of the Observer’s future plans to contribute to the work of 
the Arctic Council, with special focus on contributions to the subsidiary bodies 
through project participation and support, as well as collaboration with Permanent 
Participants; and, 

(c) If applicable, a description of the Observer’s contributions to other aspects of the 
Arctic Council and its goals not covered in the previous sections since the time of the 
Observer’s most recent submission, or in the previous two years. 

 

Observer reports should be submitted electronically to the Arctic Council Secretariat via 

email: acs@arctic-council.org not later than 1 December 2024. Please bear in mind while 

preparing your report that all Observer reports will be published online in the Observer 

section of the Arctic Council online Library (OAR) following the Chairship transition. 

If an Observer fails to submit a report, the Arctic Council will consider this to mean that the 
Observer is no longer interested in maintaining its status as an accredited Observer to 
the Arctic Council.

Observer Report 
Please describe in no more than two pages your State’s or Organization’s contributions to 
the work of the Arctic Council’s Working Groups, Task Forces, and/or Expert Groups since 
the time of your most recent report, or in the previous two years. Please highlight 
contributions to specific projects, such as through proposals, concept development, in- 
kind and financial support, and hosting of meetings. Please detail any collaboration with 
Permanent Participants, such as project proposal endorsement and support. 

UNEP has been active as an Observer to the Arctic Council since 1998, taking part in the 
Council’s Ministerial and Senior Arctic Officials meetings. Together with its collaborating centre, 
the World Conservation Monitoring Centre (UNEP-WCMC) in the UK, and GRID-Arendal in 
Norway - it has actively engaged with the Council’s scientific and technical groups. 

While UNEP does not have a formal programme in the Arctic or Polar regions, we facilitate global, 
regional and national policymaking relevant to the Arctic by providing and coordinating 
environmental assessments and making environmental data and information available on open 
platforms. UNEP also actively engages in various scientific collaborations and efforts to monitor 
emerging issues and raise awareness about a range of Arctic-related topics. 

Over the course of the last two years, UNEP has engaged the Council’s work as follows: 

Following the publication of the Scientific Assessment of the Third Pole Environment (UNEP 
2022), which provides a comprehensive assessment of the environmental changes in the Tibetan 
Plateau, Pamir-Hindu Kush, and Himalaya mountain ranges, UNEP has continued working to 
enhance resilience and regional governance of mountain regions. In this regard, UNEP and 
regional stakeholders such as ICIMOD, have learned from the regional governance experience of 
the Arctic Council and its working groups. This includes participating with an AMAP representative 
in a session of the 2nd Hindu Kush Himalaya Science-Policy Forum on 21-22 September 2023 in 
Kathmandu, Nepal. UNEP representative then participated in the International Symposium on 
Third Pole Environment during 14-17 November 2023 in Chongqing, China, with a focus on the 
themes of climate change and other environmental challenges over the Third Pole and its global 
linkages with polar regions. 

 

UNEP’s 2024 Global Foresight Report – Navigating New Horizons (UNEP 2024) identified the 
unseen dangers and potentially severe risks of ancient microbes, including pathogens, released 
from thawing Arctic permafrost as one of 18 potential global disruptions on the horizon. 
Researchers caution that these ancient microorganisms, some of which may be pathogenic, could 
have grave consequences for environmental, animal and human health. This phenomenon has 
already led to an outbreak of anthrax in Siberia, killing thousands of reindeer and affecting dozens 
of people. This emerging issue, along with others identified in the Foresight Report, are signals 
requiring monitoring. 

UNEP and GRID-Arendal (A partner organisation collaborating with UNEP) were partners in the 
organization of the Second International Symposium on Plastics in the Arctic and Sub-Arctic 
Region 22-23 November 2023 - Reykjavík, Iceland. GRID-A staff were members of the Scientific 
Steering Committee and produced the Symposium Summary https://www.arcticplastics.is . 

UNEP’s Climate and Clean Air Coalition (CCAC) is a partnership of more than 90 countries and 
100 non-state partners including the International Cryosphere Climate Initiative (ICCI), WHO and 
WMO. All 8 Members of the Arctic Council are CCAC partners. 3 Arctic Council Members 
(Canada, Norway and the United States) are currently on the CCAC Board. 6 Arctic Council 
Members (Canada, Denmark, Finland, Norway, Sweden and the United States) have been or are 
currently donors to the CCAC Trust Fund.

In 2024, the CCAC Board approved funding for a 2025 global cryosphere convening focused on 
black carbon and methane reduction for cryosphere preservation. The CCAC is currently 
developing a preliminary agenda for consultation. 

At the Climate and Clean Air Conference 2024, on the margins of UNEA6, a Science-Policy 
Dialogue on Black Carbon was held. This included a representative of AMAP speaking as a 
panellist. 

GRID-Arendal published the Arctic Permafrost Atlas in 2023. The atlas provides an overview of 
permafrost, impacts of climate change on permafrost, impacts of permafrost changes on human 
lives and livelihoods, and adaptation to permafrost change. In addition, it includes interviews with 
people who live and work in permafrost environments. UNEP and AMAP contributed to the 
external review. 

GRID-Arendal was a co-author of the State of Wildfires 2023-2024 report. GRID-Arendal was a 
co-author of the State of Wildfires 2023-2024 report and contributed to UNEPs work in this area. 
Plans are underway to publish this report on a regular basis (annual or biennial), including a 
section on policy implications and responses.

If applicable, please describe in no more than one page your State’s or Organization’s 
future plans for contributing to the work of the Arctic Council’s Working Groups, Task 
Forces, and/or Expert Groups. Please highlight intentions to contribute to specific projects 
and to collaborate with Permanent Participants. 

 

UNEP is committed to remaining an engaged Observer to the Arctic Council, supporting the 
Norwegian and upcoming Danish chairships, the working groups, and the Permanent Participants. 

UNEPs partner GRID Arendal is assisting UNEP in participation of the working groups to the 
Arctic Council along with an internal Polar group. 

The CCAC is currently leading two assessment reports relevant to the Arctic Council. The first, the 
Agriculture and Food Systems Assessment, will analyse mitigation opportunities across in the 
agrifood system and identify priority measures, at global and regional scales, which can deliver 
near-term climate, air quality and food security benefits. The Assessment will include all green-
house gases and air pollutants and is expected to be published in time for COP30. 

The second assessment is the Climate and Clean Air Economic Assessment, which will be the 
first ever assessment of the combined economic impacts of air pollution and climate change, the 
economic costs and benefits of mitigation actions, and the costs of delayed action. The Economic 
Assessment will include a number of exciting innovations, the first of which is the development of 
an air pollution impacts module for the PAGE and MAGIC models, which will allow all future work 
using these models to include air pollution (instead of only climate impacts). The second is a 
systematic barriers analysis, based on expert surveys, which will assess implementation barriers 
at a country level and the time and economic cost of those barriers – this analysis will be used to 
support the cost of inaction scenarios used for the assessment. The Economic Assessment will be 
published in early 2026. 

In 2025, the CCAC, in its role as the GMP Secretariat, along with the IMEO will publish a Global 
Methane Status Report, which will assess progress made on global methane mitigation since the 
formation of the GMP. The Status Report will develop projections, based on existing commitments 
and policies, to assess the potential mitigation in 2030 if all commitments are met. 

With the historic resolution 5/8, the United Nations Environment Assembly decided that a 
science-policy panel should be established to contribute further to the sound management of 
chemicals and waste and to prevent pollution. This outcome will be important for areas like the 
Arctic and the significant contributions of AMAP to this work. 

GRID-Arendal, the Saami Council, and NIVA have submitted two project proposals: one to 
Nordforsk, titled Árvvut – Embedding Saami Values and a Holistic World View in Policy and 
Research, and another to the Prince Albert Foundation, titled SáVaNa. The SáVaNa project aims 
to integrate diverse values of nature – identified through exploring and rediscovering Sámi 
practices – into policy for sustainability, more effectively addressing biodiversity loss and other 
environmental challenges in the Arctic. 

GRID-Arendal, together with AMAP and other partners, has submitted a project proposal to 
Norforsk, titled Co-creating water knowledge to support communities and policy development for 
ONE Arctic. 

GRID-Arendal and PAME are discussing a small contract to process further data from the Arctic 
Ship Traffic Data (ASTD). 

GRID-Arendal is discussing the production of a story map related to wildland fires in the Arctic for 
EPPR/Arctic Council Secretariat. 

There is an interest (but no funding) by UNEP and GRID-Arendal to develop a project on boreal 
forest value and conservation.

If applicable, please describe in no more than one page your State’s or Organization’s 
contributions to other aspects of the Arctic Council and its goals not covered by the 
previous sections since the time of your most recent report, or in the previous two years. 

 

UNEP regularly engages with partners in advocacy and outreach activities for the global 
cryosphere, including within the UNFCCC and CBD. For instance, there have been regular events 
with UNEP participation and support at the UNFCCC Cryosphere Pavilion, together with the 
International Climate and Cryosphere Initiative. 

In addition, UNEP actively participates in two task forces for the implementation of the 
International Year of Glaciers` Preservation 2025, based on UNGA Resolution 77/158 that was 
tabled by Tajikistan in 2022 at the 77th session. The International Year and World Day for Glaciers 
aim to raise global awareness about the critical role of glaciers, snow and ice in the climate 
system and the hydrological cycle, and the economic, social and environmental impacts of the 
impending changes in the Earth’s cryosphere, as well as to share best practices and knowledge in 
this regard and in addressing issues related to accelerated melting of glaciers and its 
consequences. In this regard, UNEP works on national, regional and global advocacy, regional 
science-policy frameworks, and disseminating new knowledge products on relevant topics of the 
disappearing cryosphere. 

Several MEAs are adopted under the auspices of UNEP (Minamata Convention on Mercury, 
Stockholm Convention on POPs). Together with the Regional Seas Programme, they provide 
important (global) mechanisms for the protection of human and environmental health, and are 
relevant for the Arctic. 

GRID-Arendal is a partner in the Horizon Europe project SEA-Quester which aims at making a 
rigorous analysis of polar blue carbon stocks and their dynamics, laying the foundations for a fit-
for-purpose blue carbon accounting with balance sheets for not only carbon sequestration, but 
other impacted marine ecosystem services such as fisheries production. The outcomes will be 
relevant for AMAP and CAFF, and maybe PAME. 

GRID-Arendal is a partner in the Horizon Europe project ILLUQ which will study permafrost thaw 
from a One Health perspective. Results are relevant for AMAP’s One Health project. 

GRID-Arendal is working on two more horizon proposals: one related to marine impacts of climate 
change in the Arctic, and one on “The Impact of Trust, Lifeline Vulnerability and Situational 
Awareness toward Efficiency in Governance and the Disaster Risk Management Cycle.” 

On 8 December 2023, the United Nations General Assembly officially established World Cleanup 
Day, which will be observed annually on 20 September. This year’s inaugural event (20 
September 2024), hosted by Tromsø, Norway—also known as the capital of the Arctic—was 
themed “Arctic Cities and Marine Litter”. The event aimed to inspire other cities and communities 
worldwide to adopt sustainable practices that protect our planet’s polar and sub-polar regions. 
This is relevant for PAME’s Arctic Coastal Cleanup-project. 

GRID-Arendal, University of the Arctic and others, published Frozen Arctic: Horizon scan of 
interventions to slow down, halt, and reverse the effects of climate change in the Arctic and 
northern regions, relevant for AMAP’s project proposal on Implications of climate interventions. 
UNEP also expressed the need to engage in a comprehensive review of emerging technologies 
and interventions.
